newsitem.title: GERMANY: German gold plan boosts EMU, knocks Bonn hard line.
newsitem.headline: German gold plan boosts EMU, knocks Bonn hard line.

text.p: Germany's about-turn decision to revalue its gold reserves improved the prospects for the European Union's single currency but undermined Bonn's drive to make it as hard as the deutschemark, analysts said on Friday.

The plan, seized upon after falling tax revenues tore a new gaping hole in Germany's 1997 budget, found no imitators elsewhere in Europe, probably because other central banks already price their reserves closer to current market levels.

But it devalued Germany's repeated stern warnings against "creative accounting" to meet the Maastricht criteria and cast further doubt over Finance Minister Theo Waigel's unswerving pledge to land on or below the three percent deficit target.
The gold market, facing the prospect that bullion may become just another asset, reacted nervously. The metal slipped to a London fix of $344.50 an ounce, down from $346.40.

"It all smacks of a German government hitting the panic button," said David Brown, chief European economist at Bear Stearns in London. "What they are actually doing is opening up the whole EMU game to creative accounting methods."

Graham McDevitt, economist at Paribas Capital Markets in London, said: "The fact that a lot more fudges are being used, rather than structural adjustments, does lend itself to the view that we could have a weaker euro."

Italy, for prudent Germans the image of fast and loose budget practices, saw its chances of joining EMU in the first wave in 1999 improve strongly since its strongest critic was visibly straining to clear the same hurdles.
"This option of keeping the Italians out of the currency union at the start seems increasingly less probable now," said Giovanna Mossetti of the Milan finance house Caboto.

Italian Foreign Minister Lamberto Dini pointedly remarked that Germany's latest moves could endanger the EMU stability pact, a package of rules and penalties Waigel insisted on to ensure sceptical German voters would accept the euro.

"I would be very surprised if the German government were to have recourse to accounting gimmicks such as the use of asset sales or a revaluation in order to meet a revenue shortfall for 1997," Dini told the International Herald Tribune.

Revaluing gold reserves has the blessing of the European Monetary Institute (EMI), forerunner of Europe's central bank, and dates back at least to 1975 when the Bank of France abandoned fixed price valuations for six-monthly adjustments.
No European central bank values its gold as prudently as the Bundesbank, which books assets at all-time lowest prices or at the purchase price according to German book-keeping rules.

Germany's move surprised analysts and markets because Bonn had long denouced one-off budget fixes and the Bundesbank had fiercely resisted an International Monetary Fund (IMF) plan to sell some of its gold to help to relieve Third World debt.
Analysts expect Germany to miss its own 2.9 percent deficit target for 1997, ending up instead with a 3.2-3.5 percent deficit which could still be seen as acceptable for EMU entry.

The revaluation of gold and currency reserves was part of a stop-gap package Waigel is working on that includes sales of Deutsche Telekom shares and government properties, further spending cuts and maybe a petrol tax increase.

Although the revenues could not flow directly into Waigel's 1997 budget deficit hole, which expanded by 18 billion marks ($10.6 billion) after a new tax shortfall estimate on Thursday, they could be used to retire old debt and thus relieve some pressure on interest payments.
Eurostat, the European Union's statistical watchdog, said it would rule on the plan when and if it became law.
German politicians and pundits were scathing about Waigel.

"With an arrogant style Waigel has accused other European countries of manipulating their budgets to meet the Maastricht criteria," said Ingrid Matthaeus-Maier of the opposition Social Democrats. "Now he is pulling the same stunt."
The mass-circulation Bild newspaper said Waigel's gold plan amounted to "witchcraft" and hooted in its headline: "The Waigel miracle -- a billion-mark hole disappears overnight."

The business daily Handelsblatt said: "The budget fever of the last days is shameful for a state of the economic ranking of Germany. It disturbs the people, drives away companies and frightens investors."

Echoing German mistrust of Italy's qualifications for EMU, Greens party leader Joschka Fischer harangued Waigel in parliament with the words: "With ideas like that, you'd be highly respected in the Palermo city hall."
